title: The 15/15 and 10/10 under the YIELD row are PRICE data scoring a candidate
status_plain: This is the sharpest attribution trap in the financial domain. Two figures, 15 of 15 identification and 10 of 10 held out, sit inside the catalogue's YIELD row. They are not YIELD's. They were measured on 25 live-Excel PRICE points across five bonds, and they score a CANDIDATE -- binexp for integer exponents, powf for fractional, coupons first -- in a sentence whose own subject is that the shipping forward kernel was wrong. Landing them on PRICE as a production figure would overclaim by a full kernel generation; landing them on YIELD would credit a surface that was never measured. They are recorded on PRICE, as candidate scores, with YIELD present only as the contrast that explains where they were found.

retractions.withdrawn_claim: the dive-plan premise "forward kernel already bit-exact, YIELD is 100% schedule"
retractions.superseded_by: The forward PRICE kernel was not bit-exact: `pcomp` computed base^(off+k) via `base.powf`, which is exp times ln even for integer exponents.

open_question: Fixing pcomp alone with the current bisection regresses the par witness from 6 to about 40 ULP, so the forward fix and the schedule have to land together. That coupling is why the YIELD row is still M2.
reader_warning: These two figures are printed inside the YIELD catalogue row but were measured on PRICE inputs and score a candidate model, in a sentence that simultaneously declares the shipping kernel wrong. They may not be rendered as a YIELD figure, and they may not be rendered as a production PRICE figure. YIELD itself has no pass-rate figure anywhere; see EV-FIN-0023.
